title: The great idler
hookLine: a teaching book tells its reader that all the reading won't settle them until they forget it all
carry: drop the doer, not the work

cards: Somewhere on a shelf there's a stack of books about letting go, and every one of them is something else to hold on to. The Ashtavakra Gita seems to know that joke.
Deep in the book, the sage says something that could make a diligent reader put the page down. You can talk about the scriptures and listen to them, my child, as much as you like.
But you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all. A book telling its reader that the reading isn't the point. And a few verses later, it praises a master of idleness.

teach.b: This is chapter sixteen, in paraphrase. After the line about forgetting, the sage goes on.
You may enjoy, you may work, you may meditate, but the mind will still long for what lies beyond all that, where wanting goes quiet.
Then something like a diagnosis: everyone is unhappy because of their striving, and nobody notices. Then a verse that can sound like a joke.
Happy is the great idler, the one for whom even opening and closing the eyes is a bother. Read straight, that's a blessing on the couch.
Many teachers read it another way, because the verses around it are about one kind of effort: the strain of the one who thinks, I am the doer. The Bhagavad Gita names that strain plainly.
Deluded by ahamkara, the ego, a person thinks, I am the doer.

teach.h: 'I DO NOTHING AT ALL,' WHILE THE WORK GOES ON.
teach.b: And the one who knows the truth, it says, thinks, while seeing, hearing, walking, even breathing, I do nothing at all.

teach.h: DROP THE DOER, NOT THE WORK.
teach.b: That's one of Hinduism's big teachings: the work goes on, and the ego's claim on it drops. So the great idler isn't someone who won't wash the dishes. The dishes still get washed; nobody inside is clenching about it.

The forgetting is read the same way. The sage isn't asking Janaka to forget his kindness or his duties. He's asking him to stop holding the teaching like a possession, one more thing for the ego to own.
The book has pointed at freedom for pages; now even the pointing drops away.

how: Some teachers of the Ashtavakra Gita read its praise of idleness, with Bhagavad Gita 3.27 and 5.8, as the end of the ego's sense of being the doer rather than of outward work; some Hindus close an action or a puja by offering it, with words like Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

o: a lazy student scolded for skipping lessons
someone who has given up all work and chores
one in whom the inner straining has stopped

p: won't settle you until you forget it all
why everyone is unhappy, says the sage
the ego that says, I am the doer
no inner clench; the dishes still get washed

s: the master idler is someone who refuses to do any work
the verses are about inner straining, the sense of I am the doer, not about avoiding chores.
the sage says scriptures won't settle you until you forget it all
you can talk about and listen to them as much as you like, he says, but rest comes when you forget.
in the Bhagavad Gita, the one who knows the truth thinks, I do nothing at all, even while acting
while seeing, hearing, walking, even breathing: the work goes on, and the ego's claim on it drops.

games.q: you've studied this path for a thousand days. the sage looks at your stack of notes. what does he say?
o: you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all.
start again from the first page.
games.why: chapter sixteen says it plainly: talk and listen as much as you like, but rest comes only when you forget it all.

practice: For these minutes, try the sage's kind of idleness: don't manage the breath, don't follow a technique, don't try to remember anything. Let breathing, hearing and seeing happen, and notice they happen without anyone pushing them.
If you catch yourself trying to sit well, let that go too. If you pray, close the way many Hindus close an action, offering it: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna.

wordCard.voice: Great idler, the one in whom the inner striving has stopped, because the ego's I am the doer has gone quiet. Today, the Ashtavakra Gita's hardest line: forget it all.

carryVoice: Your line: drop the doer, not the work. The dishes still get washed. Same time tomorrow.
